title: Polyglot SDK lazy-fragment adapters and tool-handshake v2 samples
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Implement a polyglot adapter layer that supports lazy reassembly of fragmented streaming output, a robust tool/function handshake v2, and concrete examples for TypeScript, Python, and Go. The goal is to provide ergonomic SDK primitives that can accept interleaved fragments, validate partial JSON/CBOR fragments against schemas, and surface a consistent tool-calling contract across runtimes. This ticket covers design, reference implementations, tests, and a small migration guide for existing streaming/tool integrations.
acceptance_criteria: SDK provides a LazyFragmentReader primitive in TS/Py/Go that can reassemble fragments into validated structured outputs without blocking the main event loop
Tool handshake v2: SDKs expose a handshake API that negotiates supported schema versions and chunk framing, with fallback to v1 behavior
Three reference examples (ts, py, go) demonstrating: progressive partial-object emission, a tool invocation with typed args, and graceful resume after transient network interruption
Unit + integration tests cover edge cases: out-of-order fragments, duplicate fragments, schema evolution (optional fields), and partial tool failure leading to fallback to plain text generation
Documentation and migration guide added to SDK docs; example repo PR opened and linked
notes: This work is intended as a compatibility layer rather than a breaking API change. v2 handshake negotiates features; if not supported, SDKs should revert to existing streaming framing semantics.
We favor non-blocking reassembly: the runtime should emit validated partial objects as soon as they are available rather than waiting for full sequences when possible.
Performance target: reassembly should add < 3% latency for p50 compared to current streaming baseline in microbenchmarks when fragments are small (<= 256 bytes).
decisions: Use a small binary framing header for fragment metadata (sequence id, total parts optional, schema version), encoded as base64 in TS/Go but with a human-readable JSON prefix in Python for easier debugging during rollout.
Validate fragments incrementally using the same JSON Schema files stored in model catalog; SDKs will cache schemas per-model and fall back to best-effort reconstruction if schema unavailable.
Tool handshake v2 will introduce a 'capabilities' exchange message at stream start: {"capabilities_version": 2, "supported_fragments": true, "schema_validation": true}
implementation_steps: Draft adapter API surface and interop spec (this ticket)
Implement LazyFragmentReader in TypeScript, with tests and microbenchmarks
Port implementation to Python and Go, matching runtime primitives (async iterator in TS, async generator in Py, channel-based emitter in Go)
Implement handshake v2 message in SDK client layer and update runtime to emit capability header in test environments
Add schema caching + validation helper (lightweight dependency on ajv for TS, jsonschema for Py, gojsonschema for Go)
Write migration guide and example PR that converts an existing streaming-tool example to use the new primitives
End-to-end QA with dedicated capacity cluster and flaky-network test harness
Submit cross-team review and iterate on feedback

example_snippets:
Python sample:

# consumer.py
from redwood_sdk import LazyFragmentReader, ToolClient
async def stream_handler(stream):
    reader = LazyFragmentReader(stream, validate=True)
    async for obj in reader.read_validated_objects():
        if obj['type'] == 'tool_call':
            resp = await ToolClient.invoke(obj['tool'], obj['args'])
            await reader.emit_tool_response(obj['call_id'], resp)
        else:
            print('partial', obj['payload'])
